subject: Architecture
title: Hostile Architecture: Designing Against People
description: A micro-lesson that makes Hostile Architecture: Designing Against People usable.

hook.text: Armrests on public benches aren't for comfort — they're designed to stop homeless people from lying down.

buildup.text: Hostile architecture uses spikes, sloped surfaces, and divided seating to discourage 'undesirable' behavior.

discovery.text: London installed metal spikes in doorways. Cities added bumps under bridges and removed sheltered seating.

twist.text: These designs don't solve homelessness — they move people out of sight, often into more dangerous locations.

climax.text: Public backlash is growing. Some cities are removing hostile elements and redesigning public space for everyone.

punchline.text: Architecture can welcome or reject. The bench tells you which one it chose.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of hostile architecture?
options: To improve safety by preventing accidents in public spaces
To discourage behaviors like sleeping on benches or in doorways
To reduce maintenance costs on public infrastructure

details.summary: Hostile architecture uses design features — spiked surfaces, divided benches, sloped windowsills — to prevent people from sitting, sleeping, or lingering in public spaces. Defenders call it order maintenance; critics call it a war against homeless people waged through design rather than policy.
details.whyItMatters: Hostile architecture forces a confrontation with who public space is really for. Every bench with armrests dividing it into single seats is a design decision that prioritizes control over compassion — architecture as social exclusion.
takeaways: Hostile architecture uses design to prevent lingering or sleeping
Spikes, divided benches, and sloped surfaces are common tactics
It raises ethical questions about who public space serves

faq.question: What are examples of hostile architecture?
faq.answer: Metal spikes on flat surfaces to prevent sleeping, bench armrests that prevent lying down, angled window ledges to prevent sitting, rocks under bridges, sprinkler systems on timer, and blue lighting in bathrooms to make veins invisible and deter drug injection.

faq.question: Is hostile architecture effective?
faq.answer: It displaces people rather than solving problems. Homeless individuals simply move to less visible locations, while the hostile features make public spaces less welcoming for everyone — elderly people who need to rest, parents with children, and anyone wanting to sit in a city.
